current.label: exercise
current.title: Exercise: a poisoned package release steals cloud and CI credentials from your build pipeline
current.real_story: On November 17, 2026, versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 of Microsoft's agent-framework package were published on PyPI with a credential stealer. A .pth file ran it at Python startup, even if the package was never imported. It targeted environment variables, credential files, Azure managed-identity and Azure DevOps tokens and, in 1.26.2, GitHub Actions OIDC tokens, and sent them to a webhook.site endpoint. Wiz says both versions were unavailable on PyPI by about 21:30 UTC and that 1.26.0 is the most recent safe version. BleepingComputer says it remains unclear how the attacker gained access to publish; Microsoft had not responded by publication time.

facts.text: Versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 of the agent-framework package were published on November 17, 2026 with a stealer that BleepingComputer says executed automatically during normal Python startup in affected environments, even if the package was never imported.
Wiz says 1.26.2 restored the clean __init__.py and used a new trigger (af_runtime_diag.pth), so searching only for 1.26.1 filenames will miss it.

Wiz says the stealer targets environment variables matching terms such as token, secret, key, azure, aws, github and npm, credential files, and Azure DevOps and Entra OIDC tokens; 1.26.2 adds GitHub Actions OIDC tokens for workflows with id-token: write.
Socket reports that the collected data is compressed, Base64-encoded and sent by POST to a webhook.site endpoint, and that the reported payloads do not download or execute additional code.
Wiz says its analysis of the 50 requests kept by the webhook found 17 that represent three unique successful victim exfiltrations.
Wiz says the most recent safe version is 1.26.0, and advises searching lockfiles, CI logs, virtualenvs and container images for 1.26.1 or 1.26.2.
BleepingComputer says it remains unclear how the attacker gained access to publish under Microsoft's project.
Wiz advises rotating every secret present in affected hosts and runners and notes that stolen tokens may be valid for up to 24 hours.

current.scenario: Hypothetical: Northbridge Components, a 600-person manufacturer, has a six-person platform team and a data team building an internal AI assistant in Python. A popular open-source package used by the data team's notebooks, a build runner and one production container is replaced overnight by a malicious release. Nothing breaks, because the package still works. Your cloud provider and the package index each send notices: the release was malicious, and any Python process in an affected environment may have leaked its secrets. Builds run on a self-hosted CI runner with cloud deploy permissions.

injects.title: A notice arrives
injects.text: At 07:45 a package-index notice and a vendor blog say two releases of a package you use were malicious and ran at Python startup. The data team lead says they updated dependencies two days ago but is unsure which environments pulled the new version.
injects.ask: Who owns this, and what is your first 30-minute plan to find out where the versions ran?

injects.title: Confirmation
injects.text: A lockfile search finds the bad version in one CI runner image and two developer laptops. The container registry shows a production image rebuilt that night on the runner. Proxy logs show outbound requests to a public webhook service from the runner at the time of the build.
injects.ask: What evidence do you preserve, and do you pause all pipelines now? What does a completed request versus a blocked one tell you?

injects.title: Which secrets were reachable?
injects.text: The runner held a cloud service principal with deploy rights, a container registry token, a repository token and a package-publishing token. Cloud logs show the managed identity requested tokens at an odd hour. Nobody has a full inventory of what the runner could reach.
injects.ask: In what order do you rotate secrets, and how do you rotate without breaking production deploys? How long might stolen tokens remain valid?

injects.title: Customer and auditor pressure
injects.text: A key customer's security team heard about the incident from news coverage and asks whether their data or your software releases could be affected. Your auditor asks whether a notification obligation has been triggered.
injects.ask: What can you truthfully say now, who says it, and what do you need to find out before you can say more?

injects.title: Is the build trustworthy?
injects.text: The analyst finds that the rebuilt production image was deployed before the notice. Public reports say the stealer did not download more code, but you cannot yet rule out that the stolen deploy credentials were used.
injects.ask: Do you roll back, rebuild from a clean environment, or leave it running while you check the cloud audit logs? Who decides?

injects.title: Recovery and prevention
injects.text: Secrets are rotated and images rebuilt from a pinned known-good version. The executive asks what will stop this happening again and when the incident can be closed.
injects.ask: What are your exit criteria, and which controls (pinning, hash-checked installs, a delay before adopting new releases, least-privilege runners, egress filtering) do you commit to, with owners and dates?

questions: How would you find every place a given package version ran: laptops, runners, containers, notebooks?
Which of your CI and cloud secrets are reachable by any process on a build runner, and who knows?
How do you tell a completed exfiltration from a blocked one in your logs?
What is your order of rotation, and what breaks when you rotate each secret?
How do you decide whether an image built during the exposure window can stay in production?
Which cloud and CI audit logs would you review for use of stolen tokens, and how far back?
Who may pause all pipelines, and how does that decision get made out of hours?
What do you tell customers and auditors while the scope is still unknown?
What would make you consider your build pipeline trusted again?
good_looks_like: The team searches lockfiles, CI logs, virtualenvs and container images for the bad versions, and checks for both known file names rather than only the first.
Affected environments are isolated and rebuilt from a known-clean pinned version, not cleaned in place.
Every secret present on affected hosts and runners is treated as exposed and rotated, with an owner and an order.
Proxy, DNS and egress logs are searched for the exfiltration destination and completed transfers are separated from blocked ones.
Cloud and CI sign-in and activity logs are audited for managed identities and federated credentials reachable from affected resources.
Workflows that could request OIDC tokens are identified and trusting federated credentials reviewed.
Communications to customers and auditors state only confirmed facts and name what is still being investigated.
Follow-up actions with owners: version pinning, least-privilege runners and egress restrictions.
current.adapt: Small team: drop the auditor inject, merge roles (one person as commander and cloud admin) and run 45 minutes focusing on the first three injects. Software or regulated sectors: add a question on whether shipped builds could carry the compromise and on notification duties to regulators and customers. Teams with no CI: replace the runner with developer laptops and a shared notebook server.

exercises.label: exercise
exercises.title: Exercise: a trusted third-party script on your website starts skimming your customers
exercises.real_story: On 16 November 2026 an unauthorised party exploited a flaw in the account signup flow of Optimizely Web Experimentation, impersonated users on targeted customer accounts and inserted malicious JavaScript into those customers' projects. The code was served from Optimizely's own CDN, so it looked legitimate, and it ran on page load. Researchers report it swapped copied cryptocurrency wallet addresses, skimmed payment card data from checkout forms, collected cookies and screenshots, and tried to deliver exploit kits to older iPhones and iPads. Report URI counted 178 affected organisations. Optimizely says it closed the flaw within three hours of detection, removed the code from all affected projects, that it was not a credentials breach, and that under 5% of its customers were affected.

facts.text: On 16 November 2026 an unauthorised third party exploited a flaw in the Web Experimentation account signup flow, impersonated users on targeted customer accounts and inserted malicious JavaScript into their projects.

Optimizely says the vulnerability was closed within three hours of detection, the injected code was removed from all affected projects, this was not a credentials breach, and less than 5% of its customers were impacted.

The malicious code was placed in the custom Project JavaScript field and served from Optimizely's legitimate CDN under its own certificate; it reached visitors of at least 178 organisations' websites.
The code swapped cryptocurrency wallet addresses, skimmed payment card data from checkout forms and attempted to deliver the Coruna and DarkSword exploit kits to iPhones and iPads.

Report URI found the payload was rebuilt 26 times during the day; of the affected sites it examined, 68 had no Content Security Policy, 50 had one that still allowed the theft, and only 24 had one that fully blocked it.
Optimizely's response included blocking the vulnerable path, ending sessions, revoking tokens and resetting affected accounts.
Salesforce said Optimizely scripts were disabled across its preview and production instances while it investigated.

exercises.scenario: Hypothetical. You are a mid-sized online retailer and service provider with about 600 staff, a web shop with a checkout page, and a customer login portal. Marketing runs A/B tests and analytics through several third-party tools whose JavaScript loads on every page, including login and checkout. The tags are managed by the marketing team and an outside agency; IT security has never reviewed the list, and your Content Security Policy, if any, allows broad script sources. On a Sunday, an attacker abuses a flaw at one of those script suppliers and adds code to your project in the supplier's console. For the rest of the day every visitor to your site runs it: card details typed at checkout and session cookies are copied out, and crypto addresses your customers copy are swapped. Nothing on your own servers changed. The exercise follows the next 48 hours: finding out, stopping it, working out who was exposed, and talking to customers, card schemes and regulators.
roles: Incident lead (CISO or IT security manager)
Marketing or digital lead who owns the third-party tags
Payments or finance lead (card acquirer and PCI contact)
A senior executive who can approve taking features offline

injects.title: A researcher's message
injects.text: Monday 08:30. A security researcher emails your generic contact address: a script loaded from your A/B testing supplier's CDN on your checkout page fetched code from an unknown domain yesterday. They attach a screenshot. Customer service also has two complaints about unexpected card charges.
injects.ask: Who picks this up, and what do you check in the first 30 minutes to decide whether it is real?

injects.title: The supplier confirms
injects.text: The supplier publishes a status notice: an unauthorised party injected JavaScript into some customer projects on Sunday; the flaw is fixed and the code removed; affected customers are being contacted. Your account manager has not called. Your project's change history shows an edit by a user nobody recognises.
injects.ask: Do you turn the supplier's scripts off everywhere now, only on login and checkout, or not at all, and who has the authority and the access to do it?

injects.title: Sizing the exposure
injects.text: Engineering finds the injected code ran from about 06:00 to 19:00 on Sunday. Analytics show roughly 14,000 checkout sessions and 40,000 logins in that window. Your logs only show which pages were served, not what the script did in the browser.
injects.ask: Whose card data and sessions do you treat as exposed, what evidence do you preserve, and what do you do about logged-in sessions now?

injects.title: Pressure from outside
injects.text: Your card acquirer calls: fraud on cards used at your shop is rising and they ask for a forensic report. A technology journalist lists your site among those affected and asks for comment by 15:00. Your data protection officer reminds you of the 72-hour clock for reporting a personal data breach.
injects.ask: What do you tell the acquirer, the journalist, the regulator and customers today, and what do you not yet know that you must not state as fact?

injects.title: The hard decision
injects.text: Marketing says the A/B tests drive a large share of conversions in the run-up to the holiday season and wants the supplier's scripts back on tomorrow. The supplier says the fix is in place. A strict Content Security Policy would break two other marketing tools.
injects.ask: What conditions must be met before any third-party script runs again on login and checkout, and who signs that off?

injects.title: Recovery and lessons
injects.text: A week later. Banks are reissuing cards, customers have been notified, and the regulator has acknowledged your report. The board asks what changes so this cannot happen through any supplier's script again.
injects.ask: Which three changes do you commit to, with owners and dates?

questions: Which third-party scripts run on our login, checkout and account pages today, who added each one, and who can change them in the supplier's console?
How would we find out that a supplier's script started behaving differently, and how long would it take?
What does our Content Security Policy allow on checkout pages, and would it have blocked a script sending data to a new domain?
Who has the authority and the technical access to switch off a supplier's script out of hours, and how fast can they do it?
What evidence would we need to tell which customers were exposed, and do we collect it today?
What do our contracts with tag and analytics suppliers say about notifying us of incidents and about our access to their audit logs?
How do we decide who to notify (customers, card acquirer, data protection regulator) and in what order?
What would we say publicly in the first hours when the cause is at a supplier but the harm happened on our site?
How do we separate marketing and analytics code from pages that collect payment details or passwords?
good_looks_like: The team treated changed supplier code on its own pages as its own incident, not only the supplier's, and switched the scripts off on sensitive pages within the first hour.
Someone could produce, within minutes, a list of every third-party script on login and checkout pages and who controls each.
The team audited every change to its project in the supplier's console during the exposure window and re-checked code that may have been altered, as Unit 42 advises.
Card data entered on affected checkout pages during the window was treated as compromised and the card acquirer was told early.
The team planned to remove non-essential marketing, experimentation and analytics tags from authentication and checkout pages and to collect payment details in an isolated payment frame.
The team committed to a Content Security Policy that limits which domains may load scripts and receive data on sensitive pages, with violation reports monitored.
Public statements said what was known, what was not yet known and what customers should do, without blaming the supplier or guessing at numbers.
exercises.adapt: Small team: run it in 45 minutes with injects 1, 2, 4 and 6; one person plays the agency or freelancer who manages your website and tags, and the key question becomes whether anyone in-house can switch a script off. No online payments: replace card skimming with stolen login sessions and form data from a donation, booking or patient portal, and keep the regulator inject. Public sector: replace the card acquirer with your national CERT and the citizens using an online service.

exercises.label: exercise
exercises.title: Exercise: your unpatched VPN gateway becomes the attacker's way in
exercises.real_story: From October 30, 2026, an attacker exploited PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) in the Mobile Access portal of unpatched Check Point Security Gateways, then used a Gaia privilege escalation (CVE-2026-123039) to become root. Fixes had been available since October 23. The attacker planted PHP webshells and a persistent backdoor on the gateways. In a first wave aimed at Israeli organisations, the attacker moved from a gateway to a VMware ESXi host over SSH and ran a wiper. A second wave from November 2 hit organisations in many countries with no destructive activity seen. Check Point says a couple of dozen unpatched systems were compromised and affected customers were notified. CISA added CVE-2026-123039 to its known-exploited catalogue on November 13.

facts.text: Check Point says security fixes for Security Gateway and Management were available on October 23, one week before the attacks began.
Initial access came through PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619) in the Mobile Access Portal; root came from CVE-2026-123039 in the Gaia Dynamic CLI service.
Exploitation was observed from October 30 until November 4; only a couple of dozen unpatched systems, in a single region, were compromised in the observed incidents.
The attackers deployed PHP webshells, the persistent TSGA backdoor and its TSProxy component on the gateway, then scanned the internal network.
In the investigated intrusion the attackers moved from the gateway to a VMware ESXi host over SSH using the vpxuser service account and ran the destroy_v6 wiper.
The TSGA implant can tamper with binary firewall logs; Check Point lists unexplained gaps in firewall traffic logs as an indicator to look for.
CISA added CVE-2026-123039 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on November 13, 2026, with a due date of November 16.

exercises.scenario: Hypothetical. You are a mid-sized organisation of about 800 staff with a remote-access VPN portal on your perimeter firewall. The vendor released a hotfix for a critical portal flaw two weeks ago; the change ticket to install it is still waiting for a maintenance window because the last firewall upgrade caused an outage. Your firewall is managed by a small network team and partly by an outside partner. This morning the vendor publishes an advisory: the flaw is being exploited, attackers chain it with a second bug to get root on the appliance, plant a backdoor that survives reboots, tamper with firewall logs, and in some cases move inward to virtualisation hosts and wipe them. Your gateway runs an affected version and the portal faces the internet. Nobody yet knows whether you have been hit. The exercise follows the next few days: checking for compromise, deciding whether patching is enough, protecting the hypervisors behind the firewall, and keeping the business running while the main remote-access route may be untrusted.
roles: Incident lead (CISO or IT security manager)
Managed service or firewall partner contact
Business continuity owner or a senior executive

injects.title: The advisory lands
injects.text: The firewall vendor publishes an advisory: the remote-access portal flaw you have not yet patched is being exploited, chained with a privilege escalation to root. The advisory lists indicators: odd PHP session files, a process named like a vendor component, files dropped in /tmp, and gaps in firewall logs. A national agency adds the flaw to its exploited list with a three-day deadline.
injects.ask: Who owns this right now, and what do you do in the first hour: patch, take the portal offline, or check for compromise first?

injects.title: Something is there
injects.text: The engineer checks the gateway against the indicators. There is a session file containing the published marker string, dated nine days ago, and an unfamiliar process running as root. Firewall traffic logs have a six-hour gap the same night. The hotfix would install in 20 minutes.
injects.ask: Does installing the hotfix now help or hurt? What evidence do you need to preserve before anyone touches the box, and who can do that?

injects.title: Traffic toward the hypervisors
injects.text: Netflow from the core switch shows SSH connections from the gateway's internal interface to two virtualisation hosts during the log gap. The hosts run file servers, the finance system and the backup server. One host's service account last logged in that night.
injects.ask: Do you isolate the virtualisation hosts now, knowing it stops payroll processing tomorrow? How do you confirm backups are clean and out of the attacker's reach?

injects.title: Remote staff cannot work
injects.text: You took the VPN portal offline. 300 remote staff and two suppliers who connect through it are cut off. The operations director wants it back within the hour; the partner offers to rebuild the gateway, but the replacement appliance is three days away.
injects.ask: What temporary access do you allow, for whom, and what must be true before the portal comes back?

injects.title: Outside pressure
injects.text: A trade journalist asks whether you were among the victims named in coverage of the campaign. A large customer's security team emails asking for written confirmation within 24 hours that their data was not accessed. Legal asks whether a regulator notification clock has started.
injects.ask: What do you say today to the journalist, the customer and the regulator, given what you actually know?

injects.title: A wiper note appears
injects.text: On one virtualisation host, a test virtual machine's folder now holds a note referring to political grievances and refusing any ransom. Files in that folder were overwritten with zeros. Production machines appear untouched so far.
injects.ask: Do you shut down the remaining hosts, and what is your order of recovery if you must rebuild from backup?

injects.title: Getting back to normal
injects.text: The vendor's incident team has confirmed the backdoor and published removal guidance, but recommends rebuilding the appliance from a clean image and rotating every secret it held. The executive asks for a date when it is all over.
injects.ask: What does 'done' mean here, and what will you change so the next critical edge-device patch does not wait two weeks?

questions: How long does it take today from a vendor publishing a critical fix for an internet-facing device to that fix being installed, and what holds it up?
Which of your internet-facing devices (VPN, firewall, remote access, email gateways) could you list from memory, with their software versions, and where would you check if you could not?
If a firewall can rewrite its own logs, what independent record of its traffic do you have, and who would know how to read it?
What accounts and keys does your firewall hold or reach (admin accounts, service accounts on hypervisors, VPN certificates), and how quickly could you rotate them all?
How would you run remote access for a week if your main VPN gateway had to be rebuilt?
Which outside party would you call first to examine a compromised appliance, and is that contract already in place?
How would you prove to a customer or a regulator that data was or was not taken, when the device in the middle may have been tampered with?
What is the order of recovery for your virtualisation hosts and the systems on them, and who decided it?
good_looks_like: The team treated an exploited, internet-facing flaw as an incident at once, not a routine patch, and checked for the vendor's published indicators before and after patching.
Evidence (process list, files in /tmp, session files, a configuration and log export) was preserved before the appliance was patched, rebooted or rebuilt.
The vendor's hotfix (in the real case the November Jumbo Hotfix) was applied to every gateway and management server, with internet-facing remote-access portals first.
Firewall log gaps were cross-checked against an independent source such as switch netflow, a SIEM or the hypervisors' own logs.
Hypervisor hosts and service accounts reachable from the gateway were checked, and every credential the appliance held was rotated.
Backups were confirmed to be offline or immutable and restorable before any rebuild decision was made.
Statements to customers, media and regulators stuck to what was known, with a time for the next update, and notification deadlines were assessed by legal on day one.
The team set a target time for critical edge-device patches and named who can approve an emergency maintenance window.
exercises.adapt: Small team: run it in 45 minutes with injects 1, 2, 4 and 7, and have one person play the outside IT provider who manages the firewall; the key question becomes how fast you can reach them and what your contract says. Healthcare or manufacturing: replace the virtualisation hosts with clinical or plant systems behind the firewall and add the safety officer to the room. Public sector: use the national agency's patch deadline as the regulator pressure in inject 5.
